episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want to stay sharp, stay current, and stay ahead in clinical practice. I'm glad you're here today, because we're diving into something that doesn't get nearly enough airtime in optometric continuing education, and yet it has the potential to completely change how you manage some of the most challenging posterior segment cases you'll ever see in your chair.

Today we're talking about indocyanine green angiography, or ICG angiography, and specifically why it sees things that fluorescein simply cannot. We're going to walk through the clinical scenarios where ICG becomes not just helpful, but essential. We're talking occult choroidal neovascularization, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, and choroidal tumors. By the end of this episode, you'll have a clear framework for when to reach for ICG, what you're looking for, and how to make smart referral decisions that genuinely protect your patients' vision.

Let's start with a question. Have you ever had a patient with progressive vision loss, a suspicious fundus presentation, maybe some subretinal fluid on OCT, and yet your fluorescein angiogram came back relatively unremarkable? You know something is wrong. Your clinical instincts are firing. But the FA just isn't giving you the answer. That scenario is exactly where ICG angiography earns its place in the diagnostic toolkit.

So let's lay the groundwork first. Fluorescein angiography has been the gold standard for retinal vascular imaging for decades, and it remains incredibly valuable. But fluorescein has a fundamental limitation. The dye molecules are relatively small, and they leak readily from the choriocapillaris. On top of that, the retinal pigment epithelium, the RPE, acts as a barrier that partially blocks the fluorescence signal from the choroid. So when pathology is primarily choroidal, fluorescein can miss it entirely, or at best give you a blurry, nonspecific picture.

ICG dye is different in a very important way. Indocyanine green binds tightly to plasma proteins, which means it stays within the choroidal vasculature much longer. It also fluoresces in the near-infrared spectrum, around 835 nanometers, and near-infrared light penetrates the RPE, subretinal fluid, lipid exudates, and even thin layers of hemorrhage far more effectively than the visible light used in fluorescein imaging. The result is that ICG gives you a direct, high-resolution window into the choroidal circulation that fluorescein simply cannot provide. That's not a minor technical difference. That's a clinically transformative difference.

Now let's get into the first major clinical scenario where ICG changes the game. Occult choroidal neovascularization.

In neovascular age-related macular degeneration, we classify CNV into classic and occult subtypes based on fluorescein angiography. Classic CNV shows up as a well-defined area of early hyperfluorescence with progressive leakage. It's relatively easy to identify on FA. But occult CNV is a different story. On fluorescein, occult CNV presents as either a fibrovascular pigment epithelial detachment, or as late-phase leakage of undetermined source. The boundaries are poorly defined. The source of the leakage is unclear. And that ambiguity makes treatment planning difficult.

On ICG angiography, occult CNV often reveals itself as a focal hot spot, a discrete area of hyperfluorescence in the mid to late phases of the study. These hot spots correspond to the actual neovascular complex beneath the RPE, and they can guide laser treatment, photodynamic therapy planning, or anti-VEGF injection targeting with much greater precision. Studies have shown that ICG identifies a definable neovascular lesion in a significant proportion of cases that appear purely occult on fluorescein. For your patients with neovascular AMD who aren't responding to anti-VEGF therapy as expected, or where the lesion boundaries are unclear, ICG can be the imaging modality that finally gives the treating retinal specialist the roadmap they need.

From a chairside perspective, here's what should trigger your thinking. A patient over sixty with decreased central vision, metamorphopsia on Amsler grid testing, and on fundus examination you see subretinal fluid, a pigment epithelial detachment, or subtle subretinal hemorrhage. Your OCT shows irregular RPE elevation, maybe a double-layer sign, or hyperreflective material beneath the RPE. Your FA is inconclusive or shows only late nonspecific leakage. That's your ICG moment. That's when your referral note to the retinal specialist should specifically request ICG angiography, not just a standard FA.

Now let's move to the second scenario, and this one is critically underdiagnosed in general optometric practice. Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, or PCV.

PCV is a distinct choroidal vascular disorder characterized by an inner choroidal vascular network that terminates in polypoidal, aneurysmal dilations. It was historically considered a variant of AMD, but it's now recognized as a separate entity with its own pathophysiology, its own natural history, and importantly, its own treatment implications. PCV is particularly prevalent in Asian and African American populations, though it occurs across all ethnicities. It can present in patients who are younger than your typical AMD demographic, sometimes in their fifties or even late forties.

Clinically, PCV can look deceptively like wet AMD. Patients present with decreased vision, metamorphopsia, and you may see orange-red subretinal nodules on fundus examination, which correspond to the polypoidal lesions. You'll often see large serous or hemorrhagic pigment epithelial detachments, sometimes with a notched or irregular contour. Subretinal hemorrhage can be extensive. On OCT, you may see a thumb-like protrusion at the base of a PED, which is a classic sign of a polyp, along with double-layer sign and hyporeflective spaces within the PED.

Here's the critical point. Fluorescein angiography is often nonspecific in PCV. It may show a pattern consistent with occult CNV, or it may show a branching vascular network with late staining, but the polypoidal lesions themselves are frequently not well visualized. ICG angiography is the definitive diagnostic tool for PCV. On ICG, the branching vascular network and the polypoidal lesions light up brilliantly in the early to mid phases, giving a characteristic grape-like cluster appearance. This is pathognomonic. You cannot make a confident diagnosis of PCV without ICG.

Why does this matter clinically? Because PCV responds differently to treatment than typical neovascular AMD. Anti-VEGF monotherapy has lower efficacy in PCV compared to AMD. The current evidence, including data from the EVEREST II trial, supports combination therapy with anti-VEGF agents plus photodynamic therapy for PCV, particularly for lesions with active polyps. If your patient is being treated for presumed wet AMD and not responding well, PCV should be on your differential, and ICG should be requested.

As the primary eye care provider, your role is to recognize the clinical pattern, document your findings thoroughly, and make a timely referral with a specific request for ICG angiography. Don't just write refer for wet AMD evaluation. Write refer for evaluation of possible polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, please consider ICG angiography. That specificity matters. It guides the specialist and it accelerates the diagnostic process for your patient.

Let's move to our third major category. Choroidal tumors.

The choroid is the most vascularized tissue in the body, and it's a site where both primary and metastatic tumors can develop. The differential diagnosis for a choroidal mass includes choroidal melanoma, choroidal nevus, choroidal hemangioma, choroidal metastasis, and choroidal osteoma, among others. Getting this differential right is not academic. It is life-altering for your patient.

Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults. It can present as a pigmented or amelanotic subretinal mass, often with overlying orange lipofuscin pigment, subretinal fluid, and visual field defects corresponding to the lesion location. The classic mnemonic for risk factors of malignant transformation in a choroidal nevus is To Find Small Ocular Melanoma, which stands for Thickness greater than two millimeters, subretinal Fluid, Symptoms, Orange pigment, Margin within three millimeters of the disc, ultrasonographic Hollowness, and absence of Halo. These are your clinical red flags.

Now, where does ICG fit in with choroidal tumors? Choroidal hemangiomas are a particularly important example. Circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that can cause exudative retinal detachment and significant vision loss if untreated. On fluorescein angiography, they show early hyperfluorescence, but the pattern can overlap with amelanotic melanoma, making differentiation challenging. On ICG angiography, circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas show a very characteristic early, intense hyperfluorescence in the prearterial phase, followed by washout in the late phase. This pattern is highly specific and can help distinguish hemangioma from melanoma without requiring more invasive testing.

For choroidal melanomas, ICG can help delineate tumor vascularity and extent, which is valuable for treatment planning. For metastatic lesions, which are often multiple and bilateral, ICG can help characterize the vascular pattern and extent of choroidal involvement.

Your role as the optometrist in these cases is early detection and urgent referral. Any suspicious choroidal lesion warrants prompt referral to an ocular oncologist or a retinal specialist with oncology experience. Document the lesion size, location, associated features, and your OCT findings. B-scan ultrasonography is also a critical adjunct, particularly for assessing lesion thickness and internal reflectivity. But ICG, in the hands of the specialist, will often be part of the comprehensive workup.

Let's bring this all together with some practical takeaways you can apply starting tomorrow.

First, when you have a patient with unexplained vision loss, subretinal fluid, or a PED that doesn't fit neatly into your FA findings, think ICG. Don't just accept an inconclusive fluorescein study as the end of the diagnostic road.

Second, in patients with suspected neovascular AMD who are not responding to anti-VEGF therapy, put PCV on your differential and specifically request ICG in your referral.

Third, for any suspicious choroidal mass, especially when you're trying to differentiate hemangioma from melanoma, know that ICG is part of the specialist's toolkit and mention it in your referral communication.

Fourth, document everything meticulously. Your OCT findings, your fundus photography, your clinical observations. The more information you send with your referral, the faster the specialist can move to the right diagnostic test.

And fifth, stay current. The evidence base for ICG angiography continues to grow, particularly with the advent of swept-source OCT angiography, which is beginning to provide some of the choroidal detail that ICG offers in a non-invasive format. But ICG remains the gold standard for choroidal vascular imaging, and understanding its role makes you a better clinician and a better advocate for your patients.

The choroid is not a passive bystander in posterior segment disease. It is an active, dynamic tissue where some of the most vision-threatening pathology originates. Fluorescein shows you the retina. ICG shows you what's underneath. And sometimes, what's underneath is exactly what your patient needs you to find.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you a sharper clinical lens, pun absolutely intended, for approaching choroidal pathology in your practice. If you found this valuable, share it with a colleague, a resident, or anyone in your clinical circle who would benefit.

Visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in for more episodes, clinical resources, and continuing education content built specifically for eye care professionals like you. Until next time, keep looking deeper, keep asking better questions, and keep protecting the vision of the patients who trust you with their eyes.

Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp, clinically relevant content delivered straight to their ears. I'm glad you're here, and today we are diving deep into one of the most consequential conditions you will encounter in your exam chair, week after week, year after year. We're talking about diabetic retinopathy, and specifically, how to stage it with precision, from the earliest whisper of mild non-proliferative disease all the way through to the vision-threatening chaos of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. If you've ever stood at the slit lamp looking at a fundus and asked yourself, is this mild, is this moderate, do I refer today or do I watch, then this episode is exactly for you.

Let's set the stage with a number that should stop you in your tracks. Diabetic retinopathy remains the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults in developed countries. And here's the clinical reality, most of those patients saw an eye care provider before they lost vision. Which means the staging decisions we make, the referral thresholds we apply, and the documentation we produce are not administrative exercises. They are the difference between preserved vision and permanent visual impairment. So let's get into the science and the clinical craft of staging this disease properly.

We're going to work through four main areas today. First, the ETDRS-derived severity scale and why it matters clinically. Second, what each stage actually looks like when you're at the slit lamp or reviewing your fundus images. Third, how to think through differential diagnosis at each stage. And fourth, the chairside decision-making framework that should guide your management and referral patterns. Let's go.

The Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study, the ETDRS, is the foundational clinical trial that gave us the grading system we still use today. Published in the late 1980s and early 1990s, this landmark study enrolled over 3700 patients and gave us not just treatment data but a rigorous photographic grading scale that stratified retinopathy severity into reproducible, prognostically meaningful categories. The International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale, which was derived from ETDRS data and simplified for clinical use in 2003, is what most of us apply in practice. It gives us five levels. No apparent retinopathy. Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, or mild NPDR. Moderate NPDR. Severe NPDR. And proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR. Each level carries a specific set of funduscopic findings and, critically, a specific risk of progression. Understanding that risk is what drives your clinical decisions.

Let's walk through each stage now, and I want you to picture yourself at the slit lamp with a 90-diopter lens, or reviewing a widefield fundus image, because that's where this knowledge lives.

Mild NPDR is defined by the presence of at least one microaneurysm and nothing more. That's it. One microaneurysm. These appear as tiny, discrete, round red dots, typically in the posterior pole, often near the macula. They are the earliest clinically visible sign of retinal vascular compromise. Histologically, they represent focal outpouchings of the capillary wall due to pericyte loss, which is one of the earliest cellular events in diabetic retinopathy. At the slit lamp with a 90D lens, they can be subtle. They're smaller than a dot hemorrhage, they have a more defined border, and they don't have the feathered edges you'd see with a flame hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography, if you have access to it, will show these as hyperfluorescent dots with late leakage. The annual risk of progression from mild NPDR to PDR is relatively low, around 5 percent over five years, but that doesn't mean you ignore it. It means you establish a baseline, counsel the patient on systemic control, and bring them back in 12 months.

Moderate NPDR is where things start to get more interesting and more concerning. Here you're seeing more than just microaneurysms. You're seeing hard exudates, which are those crisp, waxy, yellow-white deposits of lipid and protein that leak from damaged capillaries. You're seeing dot and blot hemorrhages, which are intraretinal hemorrhages in the deeper nuclear layers. You may be seeing cotton wool spots, which are nerve fiber layer infarcts appearing as fluffy white superficial lesions. And you may be seeing mild venous beading. The key distinction between moderate and severe NPDR is the 4-2-1 rule, which we'll get to in a moment. In moderate NPDR, you have these findings but you haven't crossed the threshold of the 4-2-1 rule. The five-year risk of progression to PDR from moderate NPDR is approximately 12 to 27 percent depending on the study population. Your follow-up interval here tightens to every 6 months, and if there's any diabetic macular edema present, your management changes significantly.

Now let's talk about severe NPDR, because this is the stage where your clinical antenna needs to be fully extended. Severe NPDR is defined by the 4-2-1 rule, and you need to have this memorized. The patient has severe NPDR if they have any one of the following three findings. Intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms in all four quadrants. Venous beading in two or more quadrants. Or intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, what we call IRMA, in at least one quadrant. IRMA are dilated, tortuous intraretinal vessels that represent shunt vessels bypassing areas of capillary non-perfusion. They look like irregular, looping vascular channels within the retina, and they are a critical sign because they indicate significant ischemia. The one-year risk of progression from severe NPDR to PDR is approximately 15 percent, and the one-year risk of developing high-risk PDR is around 45 percent. These patients need to be seen every 3 to 4 months, and a retinal specialist consultation is strongly warranted. You are not watching and waiting here. You are actively co-managing.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy represents the transition from a disease of vascular leakage and occlusion to a disease of pathological neovascularization. The ischemic retina upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, and that VEGF drives the growth of new, fragile, abnormal vessels on the surface of the retina and into the vitreous. These new vessels, called neovascularization, can arise from the disc, which we call NVD, or elsewhere in the retina, which we call NVE. NVD is particularly ominous. At the slit lamp with your 90D lens, neovascularization appears as fine, lacy, irregular vascular fronds on the inner retinal surface or extending into the vitreous. They may be subtle early on, and this is where your stereoscopic viewing technique matters. You need to be looking in three dimensions to appreciate vessels that are elevated off the retinal plane. High-risk PDR is defined by the presence of NVD greater than one-third disc area, any NVD with vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage, or NVE greater than one-half disc area with vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. These patients need same-day or next-day retinal referral. This is not a situation where you schedule a routine referral and move on. You are picking up the phone.

Let's spend a moment on differential diagnosis, because not every red dot is a microaneurysm and not every white lesion is a cotton wool spot. When you're looking at a fundus with dot hemorrhages and microaneurysms, you need to consider hypertensive retinopathy, which can produce a very similar picture. The key differentiator is the arteriovenous changes you'll see in hypertension, including AV nicking, arterial attenuation, and the distribution of hemorrhages, which in hypertension tend to be more flame-shaped and in the nerve fiber layer. Retinal vein occlusion can also produce quadrant-based hemorrhages that might superficially resemble severe NPDR, but the distribution follows a vascular territory rather than being diffuse. Radiation retinopathy, sickle cell retinopathy, and even HIV retinopathy can produce cotton wool spots and microaneurysms. Your history is your first diagnostic tool. A patient with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 9.5 presenting with bilateral dot hemorrhages is almost certainly diabetic retinopathy. But always correlate with the clinical picture.

Now let's talk about chairside decision-making, because this is where the rubber meets the road. Your staging determines your follow-up interval, your referral urgency, and your documentation. For mild NPDR with no diabetic macular edema, annual follow-up is appropriate. For moderate NPDR, every 6 months. For severe NPDR, every 3 to 4 months with retinal co-management. For PDR, immediate referral. But here's a nuance that often gets overlooked. Diabetic macular edema, or DME, can occur at any stage of retinopathy and is actually the most common cause of vision loss in diabetic patients. You need to be evaluating the macula at every diabetic eye exam. OCT is your best friend here. Spectral-domain OCT will show you subretinal fluid, intraretinal cysts, and loss of the foveal contour with a sensitivity that clinical examination alone cannot match. If you see center-involving DME on OCT, that patient needs anti-VEGF therapy, and that means a retinal specialist is involved regardless of the NPDR stage.

Your documentation also matters enormously. Use the International Clinical Severity Scale terminology in your notes. Write mild NPDR, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR, or PDR. Document the specific findings you observed. Document whether DME is present or absent. Document your referral decision and the urgency. This protects your patient, it protects you, and it creates a longitudinal record that is clinically invaluable.

One final thought before we close. Diabetic retinopathy is a disease where optometrists are often the first and sometimes the only eye care provider a patient sees regularly. That is a profound responsibility and a profound opportunity. When you stage this disease accurately, when you counsel patients on the relationship between glycemic control and retinal outcomes, when you make the right referral at the right time, you are practicing at the absolute top of your scope. The ETDRS gave us the science. Your clinical skills and your judgment are what translate that science into preserved vision for your patients.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you a sharper, more confident framework the next time you're at the slit lamp staging diabetic retinopathy. Keep asking the hard questions, keep refining your clinical skills, and keep showing up for your patients with the expertise they deserve. Until next time, keep your lenses clean and your clinical thinking even cleaner.

episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp, clinically relevant content delivered straight to their ears. I'm glad you're here today, because we're diving into a topic that sits right at the intersection of chronic disease management and sight-saving intervention. We're talking about diabetic macular edema, specifically the criteria for clinically significant macular edema, and the OCT features that should be pushing you toward anti-VEGF thresholds. If you've ever sat across from a diabetic patient, squinted at their fundus, and asked yourself, is this bad enough to refer today, then this episode is exactly for you.

Let's set the stage. Diabetes is one of the most common systemic conditions walking through your exam lane every single day. And while we spend a lot of time thinking about diabetic retinopathy staging, it's actually diabetic macular edema, or DME, that is the leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults with diabetes. Not proliferative disease. Not neovascularization of the disc. Macular edema. That fluid accumulating in the very center of the retina, threatening the photoreceptors your patient depends on to read, drive, and recognize faces. So understanding when edema crosses the line from something you monitor to something you act on, that's the clinical skill we're sharpening today.

Let's start with the foundation. The term clinically significant macular edema, or CSME, comes from the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study, the ETDRS, which was published back in the 1980s. And even though our imaging technology has evolved dramatically since then, those criteria remain clinically relevant and are still referenced in practice today. CSME is defined by three specific findings on biomicroscopic examination. First, retinal thickening at or within five hundred microns of the center of the macula. Second, hard exudates at or within five hundred microns of the center, with associated thickening of the adjacent retina. And third, a zone of retinal thickening one disc area or larger in size, any part of which is within one disc diameter of the center of the macula. If any one of those three criteria is met, you have CSME. Full stop.

Now here's where it gets practically important. CSME is a clinical diagnosis. It was originally defined using slit lamp biomicroscopy with a contact or non-contact fundus lens, typically a 78 or 90 diopter lens, or a Goldmann three-mirror contact lens. You're looking for that subtle elevation of the retinal surface, the loss of the normal foveal reflex, and the presence of hard exudates clustering near the center. Hard exudates, by the way, are those bright yellow lipid deposits that form at the outer boundary of edematous retina. They're a sign that fluid has been there long enough to leave a residue. When you see a ring or circinate pattern of hard exudates pointing toward the fovea, your antenna should go up immediately.

But let's be honest. Biomicroscopy alone has its limits. Detecting subtle central thickening with a slit lamp takes experience, and even experienced clinicians can miss early or moderate edema without objective imaging. That's where optical coherence tomography, OCT, has completely transformed our management of DME. And this brings us to our second major segment, the OCT features that define treatment thresholds.

Spectral domain OCT is now the gold standard for evaluating DME. It gives you quantitative retinal thickness measurements, structural detail of the retinal layers, and the ability to track change over time with precision that no fundus lens can match. When you're looking at an OCT of a patient with DME, there are several key features you need to identify and document. The first is central subfield thickness, or CST. This is the average retinal thickness within the central one millimeter circle on your macular thickness map. Normal CST is generally around two hundred fifty to three hundred microns, though this varies slightly by instrument and by sex, with men typically having slightly thicker retinas than women. When CST exceeds three hundred and twenty to three hundred and fifty microns, depending on your reference values, that's a flag. When it exceeds four hundred microns, you're looking at significant edema that almost certainly warrants intervention.

But thickness alone doesn't tell the whole story. You also need to look at the morphological features on the B-scan. Intraretinal cystoid spaces, those dark hyporeflective pockets within the retinal layers, particularly in the outer nuclear layer and Henle's fiber layer, are a hallmark of DME. Subretinal fluid, which appears as a hyporeflective space between the photoreceptor layer and the retinal pigment epithelium, can also be present and is associated with more severe or chronic edema. Disorganization of the retinal inner layers, sometimes abbreviated as DRIL, is a particularly important finding because it correlates strongly with reduced visual acuity and a poorer prognosis for visual recovery even after treatment. And then there's the integrity of the ellipsoid zone, that bright hyperreflective band corresponding to the inner segment and outer segment junction of the photoreceptors. Disruption of the ellipsoid zone in the foveal region is a sign of photoreceptor stress or damage, and it tells you that the edema has been present long enough to start affecting the cells you most want to protect.

So when you're sitting at your OCT workstation reviewing a diabetic patient's scan, you're not just looking at a number. You're looking at the architecture of the macula and asking, how much damage has already occurred, and how urgently does this patient need treatment.

Now let's talk about the anti-VEGF threshold, because this is where optometrists in co-management roles need to be especially clear. Vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, is the primary driver of vascular permeability in DME. Anti-VEGF agents, including ranibizumab, bevacizumab, and aflibercept, have become the first-line treatment for center-involving DME, which is edema that affects the central subfield of the macula. The landmark clinical trials, including RIDE, RISE, PROTOCOL T, and DRCR Retina Network studies, have consistently shown that anti-VEGF therapy leads to significant gains in visual acuity and reduction in retinal thickness in patients with center-involving DME.

The key clinical decision point is this. If your patient has center-involving DME with a CST above the threshold for their instrument, and particularly if their best corrected visual acuity is worse than twenty over twenty-five, that patient needs to be in the hands of a retinal specialist for anti-VEGF consideration. This is not a watch and wait situation. Every month of untreated center-involving DME is a month of ongoing photoreceptor stress. The DRCR Protocol V study did show that some patients with good vision and center-involving DME can be observed initially, but that requires close monitoring, typically every one to three months with OCT, and a low threshold to escalate to treatment if vision drops or edema worsens.

For non-center-involving DME, where the thickening spares the central subfield, the approach can be more conservative. Focal or grid laser photocoagulation may still have a role here, particularly for edema associated with focal leaking microaneurysms. But even in these cases, close follow-up and excellent documentation are essential.

Let's move into our third segment, differential diagnosis and chairside decision-making. Not every macular thickening in a diabetic patient is DME. You need to keep your differential sharp. Epiretinal membrane, or ERM, can cause macular thickening and distortion that mimics edema on OCT. Look for the hyperreflective line on the inner retinal surface and the characteristic wrinkling or traction of the inner retinal layers. Vitreomacular traction can also cause macular thickening and may coexist with DME, complicating the clinical picture. Age-related macular degeneration with subretinal fluid can look similar, though the clinical context and the presence of drusen or RPE changes will help you differentiate. And don't forget that hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and uveitic macular edema can all produce cystoid macular edema patterns on OCT that require different management pathways.

At the chair, your decision-making framework should be systematic. Start with a thorough history. How long has the patient had diabetes? What's their HbA1c? Are they on insulin? Have they had any prior laser or injection treatment? Then move to your examination. Check best corrected visual acuity carefully, because a drop in acuity is often the first symptom a patient notices. Perform dilated fundus examination with a 78 or 90 diopter lens, looking specifically for the CSME criteria we discussed. Then get your OCT. Document the CST, the morphological features, and compare to any prior imaging. If you see center-involving edema with reduced acuity, your referral should go out the same day or within the week. If you see non-center-involving edema with good acuity, schedule a follow-up in four to six weeks and communicate clearly with the patient about warning signs, specifically any sudden decrease in vision, new distortion, or metamorphopsia.

And speaking of patient communication, this is a moment to reinforce the systemic connection. Tight glycemic control, blood pressure management, and lipid control all influence the course of DME. You're not prescribing those medications, but you are the clinician who sees this patient regularly and who can reinforce the importance of working with their primary care physician or endocrinologist. Your voice carries weight in that conversation.

As we wrap up today, let's bring it all together. Diabetic macular edema is a sight-threatening condition that demands precise clinical recognition and timely action. The ETDRS CSME criteria give you a biomicroscopic framework. OCT gives you the objective data, the central subfield thickness, the cystoid spaces, the ellipsoid zone integrity, and the DRIL findings that guide your treatment threshold decisions. Center-involving DME with reduced acuity is your anti-VEGF referral trigger. Non-center-involving DME requires close monitoring and a low threshold to escalate. And your differential diagnosis skills keep you from missing the other conditions that can masquerade as DME.

Every diabetic patient in your chair is trusting you to catch this before it steals their central vision. That's a responsibility worth taking seriously, and it's one that optometrists are uniquely positioned to fulfill through consistent, high-quality retinal evaluation.

Thank you so much for spending these ten minutes with me today. I hope this episode gives you something concrete to take back into your exam lane tomorrow. For more clinical content built specifically for optometrists and eye care professionals, visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in. Until next time, keep your lenses clean and your clinical thinking sharper.

episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want to stay sharp, stay current, and stay ahead of what matters most in clinical practice. I'm glad you're here today, because what we're covering in this episode is one of those topics that can genuinely change the outcome for a patient sitting in your chair right now.

Today we are talking about wet AMD, specifically the conversion from dry to wet, and how you, as an optometrist, can recognize it before vision is lost. We're going deep into the OCT findings, the clinical signs, the differential diagnosis, and the chairside decisions that matter most. If you see patients over fifty, if you have anyone on your books with intermediate AMD or large drusen, this episode is essential listening. Let's get into it.

So let's start with the clinical reality. Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in adults over fifty in the developed world. Most of your AMD patients are in the dry form, and many of them are stable for years. But here's the thing that keeps retinal specialists up at night, and should keep us alert too. The conversion from dry to wet, from non-neovascular to neovascular AMD, can happen silently. It can happen between annual visits. And when it does, every single day without treatment matters.

Neovascular AMD, what we call wet AMD, is driven by choroidal neovascularization, or CNV. Abnormal blood vessels grow from the choroid, breach Bruch's membrane, and invade the subretinal space or the sub-RPE space. These vessels leak fluid, blood, and lipid. They cause rapid, often devastating central vision loss. The good news is that anti-VEGF therapy has completely transformed the prognosis for these patients. But only if we catch it in time. And that is exactly where optometry plays a critical, irreplaceable role.

Let me walk you through what conversion actually looks like clinically, because this is where the rubber meets the road.

Your patient comes in, maybe they're a sixty-eight year old woman you've been following for two years with bilateral intermediate AMD. She has large soft drusen in both eyes, maybe some pigmentary changes. Her best corrected visual acuity has been stable at twenty-twenty-five in the right eye and twenty-thirty in the left. She's been doing her Amsler grid at home. Today she mentions that things look a little blurry in her right eye. She's not sure when it started. Maybe a week ago, maybe two. She thought it was her glasses.

That history alone should put you on high alert. Any new visual symptom in a patient with known AMD is a neovascular event until proven otherwise. Do not dismiss it. Do not reschedule. Do not assume it's a refractive change.

Now let's talk about what you're going to find on examination. Start with your best corrected visual acuity. Even a one or two line drop from baseline is significant. In wet AMD, you may see a drop to twenty-forty, twenty-eighty, or worse, but sometimes the acuity is still relatively preserved early on, especially if the CNV is extrafoveal. Don't let a decent acuity reassure you if the history and other findings are pointing toward conversion.

Amsler grid testing is your next critical tool. New metamorphopsia, new scotoma, or distortion that wasn't there before is a red flag. Ask your patient to compare the grid in each eye separately. If they're reporting wavy lines or a gray spot, that's a clinical emergency in the context of AMD.

Now move to your dilated fundus examination. With your slit lamp biomicroscopy using a sixty or ninety diopter lens, or your indirect ophthalmoscopy, you're looking for several key findings. First, subretinal fluid. This appears as a subtle elevation of the neurosensory retina, often with a slightly grayish or greenish hue beneath the retina. The overlying retina may look slightly domed or lifted. This can be subtle, and it's easy to miss if you're not specifically looking for it.

Second, subretinal hemorrhage. This is often the most dramatic and obvious sign. You'll see a dark red or reddish-brown patch beneath the retina, typically in the macular region. It may be small and discrete, or it may be large and extend beyond the macula. Any subretinal hemorrhage in a patient with AMD is a neovascular event until proven otherwise. Do not wait. Do not watch.

Third, pigment epithelial detachment, or PED. A PED appears as a dome-shaped elevation of the RPE. On fundus exam it may look like a smooth, rounded elevation in the macular area, sometimes with an orange or yellowish color. PEDs can be drusenoid, serous, or vascularized. A vascularized PED, meaning one associated with CNV, is a wet AMD finding and requires urgent referral.

Fourth, hard exudates or lipid. In some cases of wet AMD, especially when the CNV has been leaking for a while, you'll see yellowish-white lipid deposits in the outer retina around the macula. This is a sign of chronic leakage and suggests the process has been going on longer than the patient realizes.

Now here is where OCT becomes your most powerful diagnostic tool, and I want to spend some real time here because this is where the diagnosis is made.

Spectral domain OCT has revolutionized our ability to detect neovascular AMD early, often before the patient notices significant symptoms, and sometimes before you can see anything dramatic on fundus exam. Every patient with intermediate or advanced dry AMD should be getting OCT at every visit. That is not optional. That is standard of care.

On OCT, the hallmark findings of wet AMD conversion are these. Subretinal fluid appears as a hyporeflective, or dark, space between the photoreceptor layer and the RPE. It has a smooth, dome-shaped appearance. Even a small pocket of subretinal fluid in a patient with AMD is significant and demands urgent action. Sub-RPE fluid or a PED appears as a dome-shaped elevation of the RPE band, with a hyporeflective space beneath it. The RPE line is lifted off Bruch's membrane. A type one CNV, which grows beneath the RPE, often presents as a PED on OCT. Intraretinal fluid, or cystoid spaces within the retinal layers, appears as hyporeflective cysts or lacunae within the retinal tissue. This is a sign of more advanced leakage and is associated with worse visual outcomes if untreated. Disruption of the ellipsoid zone, which is the bright reflective band corresponding to the inner segment and outer segment junction of the photoreceptors, is a sign of photoreceptor damage. The more disruption you see, the more vision has already been compromised.

One more OCT finding worth mentioning is the double layer sign. This is a subtle finding where you see a thin, irregular layer of tissue between the RPE and Bruch's membrane. It represents type one CNV, or what we now call MNV, macular neovascularization, growing in the sub-RPE space. It can be easy to miss, but it's an early warning sign of conversion.

Now let's talk about differential diagnosis, because not everything that looks like wet AMD is wet AMD, and getting this right matters.

Central serous chorioretinopathy, or CSCR, can look very similar on OCT, with subretinal fluid and sometimes a PED. But CSCR typically occurs in younger patients, often men in their thirties to fifties, and is associated with stress, corticosteroid use, and type A personality. The fluid in CSCR tends to be more bullous and shifting, and there's usually no drusen or pigmentary changes associated with AMD. OCT-A can help differentiate by showing the absence of CNV in CSCR.

Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, or PCV, is a subtype of neovascular AMD more common in Asian and African American patients. It presents with recurrent serosanguineous detachments and polypoidal lesions on indocyanine green angiography. On OCT you may see large, notched PEDs and subretinal fluid. These patients also need urgent referral and anti-VEGF, though bevacizumab and ranibizumab may be less effective than for typical wet AMD, and photodynamic therapy is sometimes used in combination.

Vitelliform macular dystrophy and pattern dystrophies can also mimic AMD on fundus exam, but the OCT and patient history will usually clarify the picture.

Now let's talk about your chairside decision-making and management, because this is where your role as an optometrist is absolutely critical.

If you identify any of the OCT or clinical findings we've discussed in a patient with known or suspected AMD, your job is to act urgently. Same-day or next-day referral to a retinal specialist is the standard. Do not schedule a follow-up in two weeks. Do not tell the patient to come back if it gets worse. Wet AMD is a time-sensitive emergency. Every day of untreated CNV means more photoreceptor loss, more fibrosis, and less chance of visual recovery.

When you make the referral, communicate clearly. Send your OCT images. Document your findings in detail. Note the baseline visual acuity, the Amsler findings, and the specific OCT features you identified. A good referral letter or phone call to the retinal specialist can expedite the process and ensure your patient gets seen quickly.

In the meantime, counsel your patient. Explain what you found in clear, calm terms. Tell them that there is an effective treatment available, anti-VEGF injections, and that the sooner they receive it, the better the outcome. Patients who understand the urgency are more likely to follow through on the referral.

For your AMD patients who are not yet showing signs of conversion, your role is ongoing monitoring and risk reduction. Patients with bilateral large drusen or unilateral advanced AMD in the fellow eye are at the highest risk of conversion. These patients should be on AREDS2 supplementation, they should be doing daily Amsler grid monitoring at home, and they should have OCT at every visit, typically every six to twelve months depending on their risk profile. Educate them on the symptoms of conversion, new blur, new distortion, new scotoma, and make sure they know to call you immediately if anything changes.

Wet AMD is one of those conditions where optometry can make a life-changing difference. Not because we're treating it, but because we're the ones who catch it first. We're the ones with the OCT, the dilated exam, the relationship with the patient, and the clinical knowledge to recognize conversion before it becomes catastrophic.

So the next time a patient with AMD sits in your chair and mentions that things look a little different, trust your training. Get the OCT. Look carefully. Act urgently. Because the vision you save may be the vision they depend on for the rest of their life.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you the clinical confidence to recognize wet AMD conversion early and act decisively. Stay curious, stay clinical, and keep doing the work that matters.
